exercise.name: Decline Sit-up

reference.title: Decline Sit up
reference.listing: Animated GIF (title and number from the catalog listing; the page could not be read from this environment, so the movement follows the exercise name and standard coaching)

equipment: Decline bench (slant board with ankle roller)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl and sit up, inhale as you lower under control.
breathing.cadence: About 1.6 s up, a short pause, about 2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1.5 s up, brief pause, 2 s down; no jerking with the arms
prescription.progression: Start the board low (10-15 degrees) and steepen it, then slower lowering, then a light plate on the chest; master the floor sit-up first

cues.text: Lie on the decline board head-down, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat on the board and hooked under the roller; fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe out, tuck the chin a little and curl the head and shoulder blades off the board.
Keep curling and sit up toward the knees; the feet stay hooked under the roller.
Pause with the chest close to the thighs; elbows stay wide.
Breathe in and roll back down slowly: low back first, then the shoulder blades, head last. Do not drop down the slope.
Rest the shoulders on the board for a moment; repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Yanking the head forward with the hands
mistakes.fix: Fingertips only, elbows wide; or cross the arms on the chest.

mistakes.mistake: Sitting up with a flat back from the hips (hip flexors only)
mistakes.fix: Curl the head and shoulders first, then sit up.
Lower for about 2 s, one vertebra at a time; the decline makes the lowering harder to control.

mistakes.mistake: Feet slipping out from under the roller or knees falling open
mistakes.fix: Hook the feet firmly and keep the knees hip width.

kinematics.measure: Trunk (pelvis to C7) from the board
kinematics.norm: From lying on the board to sitting up close to the thighs; the decline adds load because the trunk starts head-down, as in the floor sit-up the traditional version reaches more hip flexion (J Strength Cond Res 2015)
Low back curls early and stays rounded at the top (clinical opinion)
Most of the second half of the rise is hip flexion (Andersson 1997)
About 90 degrees, feet hooked under the roller and still (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1.5 s up and 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Escamilla, Lewis, Pecson, Imamura and Andrews 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379; PMC4922527)
Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Andersson, Nilsson, Ma and Thorstensson 1997, abdominal and hip flexor muscle activation during various training exercises (Eur J Appl Physiol 75:115-123; PMID 9118976)
Effect of traditional vs modified bent-knee sit-up on abdominal and hip flexor muscle EMG activity (J Strength Cond Res 29(12):3472-3479, 2015; PMID 25970493)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Lying head-down raises pressure in the head; skip the decline with uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma or a recent eye or head problem (clinical opinion), and sit up slowly at the end of the set.
Check that the roller is locked and the feet are hooked before lying back; step off the board carefully.
Full sit-ups load the low back more than curl-ups: sit-ups gave higher compression than partial curl-ups in McGill's data (McGill 1998; Axler and McGill 1997).

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion work.
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest.
Low-back discomfort: stop at a three-quarter sit-up or a crunch.
Unanchored feet shift the work toward the abdominals (smaller range).
progressions: Light plate held on the chest.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the trunk off the board and holds the pelvis as the hips flex: about 40% (upper) and 35% (lower) MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up (Escamilla 2016). In Konrad 2001 the sit-up kept rectus activity at the curl-up level while external oblique rose to about 57% MVC.
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris take over once the shoulder blades are off the board and pull the trunk up to the thighs. Flexed and supported (anchored) legs increased hip-flexor activation in hip-flexion sit-ups without changing abdominal activity (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas and rectus femoris take over once the shoulder blades are off the board and pull the trunk up to the thighs. Flexed and supported (anchored) legs increased hip-flexor activation in hip-flexion sit-ups without changing abdominal activity (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: External obliques were about 36% MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up (Escamilla 2016) and about 57% MVC in Konrad 2001; they steady the trunk on the way up and down.
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External obliques were about 36% MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up (Escamilla 2016) and about 57% MVC in Konrad 2001; they steady the trunk on the way up and down.
muscleNotes.quads_r: Rectus femoris works as a hip flexor: about 23% MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up versus 6% in a crunch (Escamilla 2016), and it was higher in the traditional (hip-flexion) sit-up than in a trunk-flexion version (J Strength Cond Res 2015).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Rectus femoris works as a hip flexor: about 23% MVIC in a bent-knee sit-up versus 6% in a crunch (Escamilla 2016), and it was higher in the traditional (hip-flexion) sit-up than in a trunk-flexion version (J Strength Cond Res 2015).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Keep the knees in line over the anchored feet (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Keep the knees in line over the anchored feet (clinical opinion).
